# Unit 2: Regulatory approval process and regulatory authorities

This unit has two parts. **Part A** follows a drug through the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) system, which the syllabus uses as the model: the Investigational New Drug (IND) application, the New Drug Application (NDA), the Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) for generics, and how changes to an approved product are handled. **Part B** describes the regulators of India, the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, Japan and Canada: how each is organised and what types of applications it receives.

Rules, forms and review times change. The figures in these notes were checked against the official texts (US Code of Federal Regulations, FDA and EMA websites, India's NDCT Rules 2019). In real work always check the current version on the regulator's website.

## Part A: Approval processes (USA as the model)

## 2.1 The overall pathway

```text
Pre-clinical data ─→ IND submitted to FDA ─→ 30-day wait (no clinical hold)
      ─→ Phase I ─→ Phase II ─→ (end-of-Phase-II meeting) ─→ Phase III
      ─→ (pre-NDA meeting) ─→ NDA ─→ filing review (60 days)
      ─→ full review ─→ approval letter or complete response letter
      ─→ marketing + Phase IV, safety reports, supplements, annual reports

Generic copy of an approved drug ─→ ANDA (BE instead of clinical trials) ─→ approval
```

## 2.2 Investigational New Drug (IND) application

**Definition:** an IND is a request to the FDA for permission to give an unapproved drug (or an approved drug for a new, unapproved use in a trial) to humans. Legally it is also an exemption that allows the drug to be shipped across state lines for clinical trials. The rules are in **21 CFR Part 312**.

### a. Types of IND

| Type | Who files / why |
| --- | --- |
| Investigator IND | A physician who both starts and conducts a study (for example to study a new use of an approved drug) |
| Emergency use IND | For an urgent situation where there is no time to file a normal IND |
| Treatment IND | Gives access to a promising drug for serious or life-threatening disease while final trials are going on |
| Commercial (research) IND | Filed by a company that intends to market the drug |

### b. Contents of an IND

1. Cover form **FDA 1571** and table of contents.
2. Introductory statement and general investigational plan.
3. **Investigator's Brochure** (summary of non-clinical and any clinical data for investigators).
4. Clinical protocols.
5. Chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) information.
6. Pharmacology and toxicology data.
7. Previous human experience, if any.
8. Additional information; investigator statement **FDA 1572** for each investigator.

### c. Process and timeline

```text
Sponsor submits IND
      │
      ▼
FDA review (medical, chemistry, pharmacology/toxicology, statistics)
      │
      ├── Safety concern ──→ CLINICAL HOLD (trial may not start / must stop)
      │                       sponsor answers → hold lifted
      │
      └── No hold within 30 days of receipt ──→ IND in effect → trial may start
```

- An IND goes into effect **30 days after the FDA receives it** unless the FDA places a clinical hold (21 CFR 312.40); the FDA can also allow an earlier start.
- An institutional review board (IRB) must also approve each study before it starts.
- During the IND the sponsor files **protocol amendments** (new protocol, changes, new investigator), **information amendments**, **IND safety reports** and **annual reports**.
- Meetings with the FDA: pre-IND, end-of-Phase-II and pre-NDA meetings help agree the development plan.

## 2.3 New Drug Application (NDA)

**Definition:** an NDA is the application asking the FDA to approve a new drug for sale in the USA. It must show that the drug is safe and effective for its proposed use, that the benefits outweigh the risks, that the proposed labelling is appropriate, and that the methods and controls used in manufacture keep its identity, strength, quality and purity. The rules are in **21 CFR Part 314**; the application form is **FDA 356h**.

### a. Types of NDA (sections of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act)

| Route | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| 505(b)(1) "stand-alone" NDA | New molecule; the applicant owns or has right of reference to all the safety and efficacy studies |
| 505(b)(2) NDA | Relies partly on studies the applicant did not do (published literature or FDA's earlier findings), e.g. new salt, new dosage form, new combination, new route |
| 505(j) ANDA | Generic copy, shown bioequivalent to the reference listed drug |
| BLA (Public Health Service Act) | Biological products such as vaccines, blood products, monoclonal antibodies |

### b. Contents

Organised in the CTD format (Unit 3): administrative documents and proposed labelling; summaries; quality (CMC); non-clinical study reports; clinical study reports with statistical analysis; patent information; financial disclosure of investigators; case report tabulations.

### c. NDA review process and timelines

```text
NDA received
   → Filing review: FDA decides within 60 days whether the application is
     complete enough to be reviewed (else "refuse to file")
   → Review by discipline: medical, statistics, clinical pharmacology,
     pharmacology/toxicology, chemistry/manufacturing, microbiology
   → Inspections: manufacturing sites (pre-approval inspection) and
     clinical sites; labelling negotiation; advisory committee if needed
   → Action: APPROVAL LETTER  or  COMPLETE RESPONSE LETTER (deficiencies)
```

- Review goals under the user-fee programme (PDUFA): **standard review 10 months, priority review 6 months**. For a new molecular entity the clock runs from the 60-day filing date. Priority review is for drugs that would be a significant improvement in a serious condition.
- Expedited programmes: fast track, breakthrough therapy, accelerated approval (based on a surrogate endpoint) and priority review.

## 2.4 Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA)

**Definition:** an ANDA is the application for approval of a **generic** drug under section 505(j). It is "abbreviated" because it does not repeat the non-clinical and clinical studies; it shows instead that the generic is the same as the reference listed drug (RLD) and bioequivalent to it.

### a. What an ANDA must show

1. Same active ingredient(s), dosage form, strength, route of administration and conditions of use as the RLD.
2. Labelling the same as the RLD (except permitted differences, such as manufacturer and carved-out patented uses).
3. **Bioequivalence** to the RLD (or a justified biowaiver).
4. Full chemistry, manufacturing and controls data, stability and GMP compliance of the sites.
5. **Patent certification** for each patent listed for the RLD in the Orange Book.

### b. Patent certifications

| Certification | Statement | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paragraph I | No patent information has been filed | Approval possible when ready |
| Paragraph II | The patent has expired | Approval possible when ready |
| Paragraph III | The patent will expire on a stated date | Approval effective after expiry |
| Paragraph IV | The patent is invalid or will not be infringed by the generic | Patent owner may sue; if sued in time, approval is generally stayed for up to 30 months; first successful filer may get 180-day exclusivity |

A **section viii statement** is used when the generic leaves out ("carves out") a patented method of use from its label.

### c. ANDA process

```text
ANDA submitted → receipt/filing review (completeness) → review of
bioequivalence, chemistry/manufacturing, labelling, microbiology (sterile)
→ facility inspections → approval (full or tentative) or complete response
```

**Tentative approval:** the ANDA meets all scientific requirements but final approval is blocked by patents or exclusivity. Review goals are set under the generic drug user-fee programme (GDUFA); check the current FDA figures.

### d. NDA vs ANDA

| Point | NDA | ANDA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section | 505(b) | 505(j) |
| Clinical efficacy trials | Required | Not required |
| Non-clinical studies | Required | Not required |
| Bioequivalence | Not the main evidence | Main evidence |
| Cost and time | Very high, long | Lower, shorter |
| Labelling | Developed by sponsor | Same as RLD |
| Patent certification | Not applicable | Required |

## 2.5 Changes to an approved NDA / ANDA

After approval, the holder must tell the FDA about changes in components, manufacturing site, process, specifications, container closure, labelling and so on. **21 CFR 314.70** sets the categories for NDAs; **314.97** applies the same rules to ANDAs. The category depends on how likely the change is to affect the identity, strength, quality, purity or potency of the drug.

| Change | Filing | When the change may be used | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Major** | **Prior approval supplement (PAS)** | Only after FDA approves the supplement | Change in formulation (including inactive ingredients); change in sterilisation method; change in API synthesis that may alter the impurity profile; new indication (efficacy supplement) |
| **Moderate** | **Supplement – Changes Being Effected in 30 days (CBE-30)** | 30 days after FDA receives it, unless FDA objects | Container closure change not affecting quality; relaxing a specification to match an official compendium |
| **Moderate (FDA-designated)** | **Supplement – Changes Being Effected (CBE-0)** | On receipt by FDA | Adding a specification or tightening controls; strengthening a safety warning in labelling |
| **Minor** | **Annual report** | Immediately; reported in the next annual report | Changes to comply with a compendium; replacing equipment with equipment of the same design and principle; deleting a colouring-only ingredient |

FDA guidance documents (for example the SUPAC guidances for immediate-release, modified-release and semisolid products) explain which change falls in which level and what data (dissolution, stability, BE) are needed.

## Part B: Regulatory authorities and agencies

## 2.6 India — CDSCO

**Law:** Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Drugs Rules, 1945; New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019; Medical Devices Rules, 2017.

**Organisation:**

```text
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
        └── Directorate General of Health Services
               └── CDSCO, headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI)
                    = Central Licensing Authority (CLA)
                    ├── HQ divisions: new drugs, clinical trials, biologicals,
                    │   medical devices, import/registration, pharmacovigilance
                    ├── Zonal, sub-zonal and port offices
                    ├── Central drug testing laboratories
                    └── Subject Expert Committees (advise on applications)
Advisory: Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB), Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC)
States: State Licensing Authorities — manufacturing and sale licences
```

**Types of applications (central):**

| Application | Under |
| --- | --- |
| Permission to conduct a clinical trial of a new drug / investigational new drug (application Form CT-04, permission Form CT-06) | NDCT Rules 2019 |
| Permission to import a new drug for sale (Form CT-18) or manufacture a new drug formulation for sale (Form CT-21) | NDCT Rules 2019 |
| BA/BE study permission, ethics committee registration (Form CT-01, granted in CT-02) | NDCT Rules 2019 |
| Registration certificate and import licence for imported drugs | Drugs Rules 1945 |
| Test licence (small quantities for testing or trials) | Drugs Rules / NDCT Rules |
| Joint approval of licences for vaccines, blood products, large-volume parenterals, r-DNA products | Drugs Rules 1945 |

**Timelines (NDCT Rules 2019):** decision on a clinical trial application within **90 working days**; for a drug discovered and developed in India and to be manufactured in India, **30 working days**, after which permission is deemed granted if there is no communication. Applications are filed online through CDSCO's **SUGAM** portal.

## 2.7 United States — FDA

**Law:** Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (1938, with later amendments); Public Health Service Act (biologics); regulations in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

**Organisation:** the FDA is an agency of the Department of Health and Human Services, headed by the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, with headquarters at Silver Spring, Maryland.

| Centre | Regulates |
| --- | --- |
| CDER — Center for Drug Evaluation and Research | Prescription and OTC drugs, generics, most therapeutic biologics such as monoclonal antibodies |
| CBER — Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research | Vaccines, blood products, cell and gene therapies |
| CDRH — Center for Devices and Radiological Health | Medical devices |
| CVM — Center for Veterinary Medicine | Animal drugs and feeds |
| Others | Food, tobacco products; field staff for inspections |

Within CDER, the Office of New Drugs reviews NDAs and the Office of Generic Drugs reviews ANDAs. Independent **advisory committees** of outside experts give non-binding advice.

**Types of applications:** IND, NDA (505(b)(1), 505(b)(2)), ANDA, BLA (including biosimilars), OTC monograph route, supplements, Drug Master Files (Unit 3).

## 2.8 European Union — EMA and national authorities

**Organisation:** the **European Medicines Agency (EMA)**, based in Amsterdam, coordinates scientific evaluation for the EU. It works through scientific committees, mainly:

| Committee | Role |
| --- | --- |
| CHMP — Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use | Gives the opinion on human medicine applications |
| PRAC — Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee | Safety and risk management |
| CAT — Committee for Advanced Therapies | Gene, cell and tissue therapies |
| COMP — Committee for Orphan Medicinal Products | Orphan designations |
| PDCO — Paediatric Committee | Paediatric investigation plans |
| HMPC — Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products | Herbal medicines |

The **European Commission** grants the legally binding marketing authorisation. Each member state also has its own **national competent authority** (for example in Germany, France), which handles national procedures and clinical trial approvals.

**Procedures for marketing authorisation:**

| Procedure | Use | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Centralised | Compulsory for biotech products, advanced therapies, orphan drugs and new substances for certain diseases (such as cancer, diabetes, HIV); optional for other innovative products | One authorisation valid in all EU member states |
| Decentralised | Product not yet authorised in any member state; applied in several at once with one reference member state | National authorisations in each chosen state |
| Mutual recognition | Product already authorised in one member state; others recognise it | National authorisations |
| National | Product for one member state only | One national authorisation |

**Centralised timeline:** CHMP evaluation takes up to **210 active days** (the clock stops while the applicant answers questions); the European Commission then decides within **67 days** of receiving the CHMP opinion. An EU marketing authorisation is valid for five years and then must be renewed.

**Types of application (by legal basis):** full (stand-alone) application, generic, hybrid, biosimilar, well-established use (based on literature), fixed-combination, and informed-consent applications.

## 2.9 United Kingdom — MHRA

The **Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)** is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care. Since the UK left the EU it grants UK-wide marketing authorisations itself. The independent **Commission on Human Medicines** advises ministers and the MHRA. The MHRA also regulates clinical trials and medical devices, runs the **Yellow Card** scheme for reporting suspected adverse reactions, and controls GMP and GDP. Routes include national applications, and reliance routes that use decisions of other trusted regulators (check the MHRA website for the current options).

## 2.10 Australia — TGA

The **Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)** is part of the Australian Government Department of Health and regulates under the **Therapeutic Goods Act 1989**. A product must be entered on the **Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG)** before supply.

| Type | Meaning | Label number |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered medicines | Higher risk: prescription and many OTC medicines; full evaluation of quality, safety and efficacy | AUST R |
| Listed medicines | Low risk (many complementary medicines); only permitted low-risk ingredients and claims | AUST L |

Prescription medicine applications include new chemical entities, extensions of indications, and generic medicines. The TGA also takes part in work-sharing with other regulators (such as the Access Consortium with Canada, Singapore, Switzerland and the UK). Clinical trials are run under notification (CTN) or approval (CTA) schemes.

## 2.11 Japan — MHLW and PMDA

Japan has a two-tier system:

```text
Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) — grants approval, sets policy
        │ consults
Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) — scientific review,
  GMP/GCP inspections, consultations, safety measures, relief services
```

**Law:** the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act (PMD Act), which replaced the earlier Pharmaceutical Affairs Law. Advice is also given by the Pharmaceutical Affairs Council.

**Types of applications:** new drug applications (new active ingredient, new combination, new route, new indication, new dosage form), generic (follow-on) drug applications, OTC drugs and quasi-drugs. Clinical trial notifications go to the PMDA. Japan uses the CTD, with a Japan-specific Module 1. Foreign data may be accepted with a bridging approach (ICH E5) showing that the results apply to Japanese patients.

## 2.12 Canada — Health Canada

**Health Canada**, through its Health Products and Food Branch, regulates drugs under the **Food and Drugs Act and Food and Drug Regulations**. Within it, the Therapeutic Products Directorate (pharmaceuticals) and the Biologic and Radiopharmaceutical Drugs Directorate (biologics) review submissions.

| Submission | Use |
| --- | --- |
| New Drug Submission (NDS) | New drug, full data |
| Abbreviated New Drug Submission (ANDS) | Generic, comparison with a Canadian reference product |
| Supplemental NDS / ANDS | Changes such as new indication or new strength |
| Clinical Trial Application (CTA) | Permission for a clinical trial |
| DIN application | For products not classed as new drugs |

Approval of an NDS or ANDS gives a **Notice of Compliance (NOC)**, and the product receives a **Drug Identification Number (DIN)** that must appear on the label.

## 2.13 Comparison table

| Country / region | Authority | Main law | New drug application | Generic application | Approval document |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| India | CDSCO (DCGI) | D&C Act 1940; NDCT Rules 2019 | CT-18 / CT-21 with CTD | Application to CLA while still a "new drug"; else State licence | Permission from CLA; State licence |
| USA | FDA (CDER/CBER) | FD&C Act; 21 CFR | NDA / BLA | ANDA | Approval letter |
| EU | EMA + European Commission; national authorities | EU directives and regulations | MAA (centralised/decentralised/MRP/national) | Generic MAA | Marketing authorisation |
| UK | MHRA | Human Medicines Regulations | MAA | Generic MAA | Marketing authorisation |
| Australia | TGA | Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 | Registration on ARTG | Generic registration | ARTG entry (AUST R) |
| Japan | MHLW + PMDA | PMD Act | J-NDA | Generic application | MHLW approval |
| Canada | Health Canada | Food and Drugs Act | NDS | ANDS | NOC + DIN |

Global harmonisation bodies: **ICH** (International Council for Harmonisation — Q, S, E and M guidelines), **WHO** (guidelines, prequalification, certification scheme), **PIC/S** (GMP inspection co-operation).

## Remember

- IND: 21 CFR 312, Form 1571 (sponsor) and 1572 (investigator); four types; in effect 30 days after receipt unless clinical hold.
- NDA: 21 CFR 314, Form 356h; 505(b)(1), 505(b)(2); filing decision within 60 days; review goals 10 months standard, 6 months priority.
- ANDA: 505(j); same API, form, strength, route, use + BE; Paragraph I–IV; 30-month stay; 180-day exclusivity; tentative approval.
- Changes: major = PAS; moderate = CBE-30 or CBE-0; minor = annual report (314.70; 314.97 for ANDA).
- India: CDSCO/DCGI; CT-04 → CT-06; CT-18 import, CT-21 manufacture; 90 working days (30 for India-developed); SUGAM.
- USA: FDA under HHS; CDER, CBER, CDRH, CVM.
- EU: EMA (CHMP, PRAC, CAT, COMP, PDCO); Commission grants; centralised, decentralised, mutual recognition, national; 210 active days + 67 days.
- UK MHRA (Yellow Card); Australia TGA (ARTG, AUST R/AUST L); Japan MHLW + PMDA (PMD Act); Canada Health Canada (NDS, ANDS, NOC, DIN).

# Unit 3: Registration of Indian drug products in overseas markets

India exports medicines to almost every country in the world, mostly generics. To sell in another country, an Indian company must satisfy two sets of rules: **Indian export rules** (licences, certificates, customs) and the **registration rules of the importing country** (a dossier reviewed by that country's regulator). This unit covers the export procedure, the technical documents that make up a registration dossier, Drug Master Files, and the three common dossier formats: CTD, eCTD and the ASEAN Common Technical Dossier (ACTD).

Export procedures and document lists change through notices of the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), CDSCO and importing countries. Learn the principles for the exam; in real work check the current notices.

## 3.1 Why overseas registration is needed

- No country allows a medicine to be sold unless its own regulator has authorised it (registration, marketing authorisation, approval).
- The importing regulator wants proof of **quality** (GMP, specifications, stability for its climate), **safety and efficacy** (for generics, bioequivalence with its own reference product) and **correct labelling** in its language.
- Markets are often grouped as **regulated** (USA, EU, UK, Japan, Australia, Canada — strict review and inspections), **semi-regulated / emerging** (many countries of Asia, Africa, Latin America, the CIS, the Gulf) and markets that rely heavily on WHO certificates and **WHO prequalification**.

## 3.2 Procedure for export of pharmaceutical products from India

### a. Requirements on the Indian side

| Requirement | Issued by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Importer-Exporter Code (IEC) | DGFT (Ministry of Commerce) | Needed by every exporter |
| Registration-cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC) | Pharmexcil (Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India) | Registration with the export promotion council for pharmaceuticals; needed to claim export benefits |
| Manufacturing licence | State Licensing Authority (with central approval for specified products) | Legal manufacture of the product in India |
| WHO-GMP certificate | State Licensing Authority / CDSCO after inspection | Shows the site follows WHO GMP |
| Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product (COPP) | CDSCO (zonal offices), in the WHO certification scheme format | Required by many importing regulators |
| Free sale certificate, market standing, non-conviction and similar certificates | Licensing authorities | Asked by some importing countries |
| Export NOC | CDSCO (port office) | For export of drugs not approved for sale in India, or of unapproved new drugs and certain other categories; check current rules |

Other points: export packs may need special labelling (for example "For export only"), and DGFT has rules on track-and-trace barcoding of export packs; drugs controlled under the NDPS Act need separate export authorisation from the Narcotics Commissioner.

### b. Steps in exporting a product

```text
Market selection (demand, competition, regulatory route, patents)
   → Appoint local agent / importer / marketing authorisation holder
   → Study importing country's registration rules (dossier format, BE
     reference product, stability zone, labelling, fees)
   → Prepare dossier (CTD / ACTD / country format) + samples + certificates
     (COPP, GMP, free sale, analysis certificates)
   → Submit to importing regulator → queries → possible GMP inspection
     of the Indian site → product registration (licence) granted
   → Import permit / import licence for each shipment (importer's side)
   → Commercial export: purchase order, manufacture, release by QA,
     export documents, customs clearance, shipment
   → Post-registration: variations, renewals, pharmacovigilance
```

### c. Shipping and commercial documents

| Document | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial invoice and packing list | Value, quantity and packing details |
| Shipping bill | Customs export declaration in India |
| Bill of lading / airway bill | Transport contract and receipt |
| Certificate of origin | Shows goods were made in India (for duty purposes) |
| Certificate of analysis (CoA) | Batch test results |
| Insurance certificate, letter of credit documents | Commercial and payment security |
| Import permit of buyer's country | Some countries need it for each consignment |

## 3.3 Technical documentation

The **technical documentation** (dossier) is the full set of scientific and administrative documents submitted to the importing regulator.

| Part | Typical contents |
| --- | --- |
| Administrative | Application form, fees, power of attorney for local agent, manufacturing licence, GMP certificate, COPP, free sale certificate, labels and leaflet in the local language, product information (summary of product characteristics) |
| Quality (CMC) | Drug substance: manufacturer, synthesis, specifications, impurities, stability (often via a DMF or certificate); drug product: composition, pharmaceutical development, manufacturing process and controls, process validation, excipient control, finished product specifications and test methods with validation, container closure, stability in the right climatic zone |
| Non-clinical | For generics: usually literature-based overview; for new products: full reports |
| Clinical | For generics: bioequivalence study report against the reference product accepted by that country (or a biowaiver justification); for new products: full clinical data |

Supporting documents commonly requested: **Site Master File** (description of the manufacturing site and its quality systems), validation master plan, batch manufacturing records, analytical method validation reports, and samples with reference standards.

### Stability and climatic zones

Stability conditions depend on the climate of the importing country (ICH and WHO zones: zone I temperate to zone IV hot and humid). A product for a hot humid country needs data under the zone IV conditions accepted by that regulator. Check the importing country's guideline for the exact conditions and duration.

## 3.4 Drug Master File (DMF)

**Definition:** a DMF is a confidential, detailed document submitted to a regulator by a manufacturer (usually of an API, excipient or packaging material) giving information about facilities, processes and materials used in making a drug component. It lets the supplier protect its confidential know-how while still allowing the regulator to review it in support of a customer's application.

### a. How a DMF works (US system)

```text
API maker (DMF holder) ──files DMF──→ FDA (DMF number allotted)
        │
        └──Letter of Authorisation (LoA)──→ Finished-product company (applicant)
                                             │
                                             └── cites DMF number + LoA in its
                                                 ANDA / NDA ──→ FDA reviews DMF
                                                                 with the application
```

- The FDA **neither approves nor disapproves** a DMF; it reviews it only when an application refers to it.
- The holder must keep it current: amendments for changes and annual reports.
- The applicant gets an "open part" (non-confidential) of the information; the "closed part" goes only to the regulator.
- For generic APIs supporting ANDAs, US law adds a DMF fee and a completeness assessment (GDUFA).

### b. Types of US DMF

| Type | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| Type I | Manufacturing site, facilities, operating procedures and personnel — **no longer used** |
| Type II | Drug substance (API), drug substance intermediate and materials used in their preparation, or drug product |
| Type III | Packaging material |
| Type IV | Excipient, colourant, flavour, essence, or material used in their preparation |
| Type V | FDA-accepted reference information |

Type II is by far the most common; Indian API makers hold a large number of US Type II DMFs.

### c. Contents of a Type II DMF (outline)

1. Administrative: holder name and address, agent, letter of commitment, list of customers authorised.
2. General information of the substance: nomenclature, structure, properties.
3. Manufacture: manufacturer and site, flow chart and description of synthesis, control of materials, critical steps and intermediates, process validation.
4. Characterisation: proof of structure, impurities (organic, inorganic, residual solvents, genotoxic impurities).
5. Control of drug substance: specifications, analytical methods, method validation, batch analyses.
6. Reference standards, container closure system, stability data.

It is now submitted in CTD format (usually Module 3.2.S plus Module 1 and the quality summary) and, for the FDA, electronically.

### d. DMF equivalents in other regions

| Region | System |
| --- | --- |
| EU | **Active Substance Master File (ASMF)**, with an applicant's part and a restricted part; or a **Certificate of Suitability (CEP)** from EDQM showing the API complies with the European Pharmacopoeia monograph |
| Canada | Master files with Health Canada |
| Japan | Master File system |
| WHO prequalification | API master file procedure |

## 3.5 Common Technical Document (CTD)

**Definition:** the CTD is an internationally agreed format for organising the quality, safety and efficacy information in a registration application. It was developed by ICH (guideline **M4**) and is used by the USA, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, the UK, India and many other countries. It standardises the **format**, not the data requirements: each country still decides what studies it needs.

### a. Structure: the CTD triangle

```text
                         /\
                        /  \
                       / M1 \      Regional administrative information
                      /------\     (not part of the harmonised CTD)
                     /   M2   \    CTD summaries
                    /----------\
                   /  M3 | M4 | M5\  Quality | Non-clinical | Clinical
                  /------+----+----\       study reports
```

| Module | Title | Main contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Administrative and prescribing information (regional) | Application forms, fees, cover letter, proposed labels and product information, country-specific certificates |
| 2 | Common technical document summaries | 2.1 table of contents; 2.2 introduction; 2.3 quality overall summary; 2.4 non-clinical overview; 2.5 clinical overview; 2.6 non-clinical written and tabulated summaries; 2.7 clinical summary |
| 3 | Quality | 3.1 table of contents; 3.2 body of data — 3.2.S drug substance, 3.2.P drug product, 3.2.A appendices, 3.2.R regional; 3.3 literature references |
| 4 | Non-clinical study reports | Pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, toxicology; literature |
| 5 | Clinical study reports | Tabular listing; biopharmaceutic (BA/BE) studies; PK and PD studies; efficacy and safety studies; post-marketing experience; case report forms; literature |

ICH sub-guidelines: **M4Q** (quality), **M4S** (safety), **M4E** (efficacy).

### b. Advantages

1. One dossier, reused for many countries with only Module 1 changed.
2. Saves time and cost of reformatting.
3. Easier review; reviewers know where to find each item.
4. Better exchange of information between regulators.
5. Basis for electronic submission (eCTD).

## 3.6 Electronic Common Technical Document (eCTD)

**Definition:** the eCTD is the electronic form of the CTD, defined by ICH (developed under the ICH M2 work on electronic standards). It lets the dossier be submitted, reviewed and kept up to date electronically through the whole life of the product.

### a. Key features

| Feature | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Folder structure | Fixed folders m1 to m5 matching the CTD modules |
| XML backbone | An index file that lists every document, its location and its life-cycle status |
| Documents | Mostly PDF files with bookmarks and hyperlinks |
| Sequences | Each submission is a numbered sequence (0000 for the first, 0001, 0002 …) |
| Life-cycle operations | Each document is marked **new**, **replace**, **append** or **delete**, so the regulator sees the current version and the history |
| Checksums | Each file has a checksum so changes or corruption can be detected |
| Regional Module 1 | Each regulator publishes its own Module 1 specification |
| Validation | Regulators check submissions with technical validation criteria before review |

The long-used version is eCTD **3.2.2**; ICH has also issued **eCTD v4.0**, based on a newer messaging standard, which regulators are bringing in step by step.

### b. Advantages over paper

- Faster submission and review; no printing, shipping or storage of paper volumes.
- Clear life-cycle management of variations and renewals.
- Easy searching and hyperlinking between summaries and reports.
- Reduced errors and duplication.

The FDA requires the eCTD format for NDAs, ANDAs, BLAs, commercial INDs and master files (check the FDA eCTD page for exceptions); the EU and other major regulators also use it. In India, CDSCO accepts dossiers in CTD format through SUGAM; check its notices for the current electronic requirements.

## 3.7 ASEAN Common Technical Dossier (ACTD)

The syllabus calls it the ASEAN Common Technical Document; its official name is the **ASEAN Common Technical Dossier (ACTD)**. It is the registration format agreed by the member states of the **Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)** (for example Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam). It goes together with the **ASEAN Common Technical Requirements (ACTR)**, which describe what data are needed.

### Structure: four parts

| Part | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Part I | Table of contents, administrative data and product information (application form, labels, package insert, product information, certificates) |
| Part II | Quality document |
| Part III | Non-clinical document |
| Part IV | Clinical document |

### CTD vs ACTD

| Point | ICH CTD | ACTD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developed by | ICH | ASEAN |
| Organisation | 5 modules | 4 parts |
| Summaries | Separate Module 2 | Overviews and summaries placed within each part |
| Administrative data | Module 1, regional | Part I, common to ASEAN with country additions |
| Generic products | Quality + BE as required by each region | Non-clinical and clinical parts often not required for generics; quality and BE (where the country requires it) are the focus |
| Electronic version | eCTD | Mainly paper/electronic files per country practice |

## 3.8 Practical tips for Indian exporters

1. Check patent and exclusivity status in each target country before development.
2. Use the importing country's reference product for BE, or confirm that a foreign reference is accepted.
3. Generate stability data at the right climatic zone conditions from the start.
4. Keep one "core" CTD dossier and adapt Module 1 or the ACTD Part I for each country.
5. Expect foreign GMP inspections (FDA, EU authorities, WHO prequalification) and keep the site inspection-ready.
6. Maintain the registration: variations, renewals, pharmacovigilance and labelling updates.

## Remember

- Export from India: IEC (DGFT), RCMC (Pharmexcil), manufacturing licence, WHO-GMP, COPP (CDSCO), free sale certificate, export NOC where needed; then the importing country's registration and import permit.
- Technical dossier: administrative + quality + non-clinical + clinical (for generics, BE); Site Master File; stability by climatic zone.
- DMF: confidential, neither approved nor disapproved; LoA lets the applicant cite it; Types II (API), III (packaging), IV (excipients), V (reference information); Type I no longer used. EU equivalents: ASMF and CEP.
- CTD (ICH M4): M1 regional, M2 summaries, M3 quality, M4 non-clinical, M5 clinical; format, not content, is harmonised.
- eCTD: folders m1–m5, XML backbone, sequences 0000…, life-cycle operations new/replace/append/delete, checksums; versions 3.2.2 and 4.0.
- ACTD: ASEAN; four parts (I admin and product information, II quality, III non-clinical, IV clinical) with ACTR.

# Unit 4: Clinical trials

A **clinical trial** is a systematic study of a drug (or other intervention) in human subjects to find or confirm its clinical, pharmacological or adverse effects, or its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, with the aim of establishing safety and efficacy. Because people are exposed to an unproven medicine, trials are controlled by law and by the ethical and scientific standard called **Good Clinical Practice (GCP)**.

Key documents for this unit:

| Document | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| ICH E6 — Guideline for Good Clinical Practice (revised as R2 and, most recently, R3) | International GCP standard |
| ICH E2A | Definitions and expedited reporting of safety data in trials |
| Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association) | Ethical principles for research on humans |
| India: New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019 | Permission, ethics committees, informed consent, safety reporting, compensation |
| India: ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research | Ethics guidance |
| USA: 21 CFR Parts 50 (informed consent), 56 (IRBs), 312 (IND) | US rules |

## 4.1 The people involved

```text
          Regulator (CDSCO / FDA …) ── permission, inspections
                     │
Sponsor ── funds, designs, manages ──→ Investigator + site team ←── Subjects
   │        (may delegate to a CRO)          │                        (consent)
   └── Monitor (CRA) checks the site ────────┘
                     │
   Ethics committee / IRB ── approves protocol and consent, watches safety
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Person, company or institution that starts, manages and/or finances the trial |
| Contract research organisation (CRO) | Organisation that does some of the sponsor's trial duties under contract |
| Investigator (principal investigator) | Qualified person responsible for conducting the trial at a site |
| Monitor / clinical research associate (CRA) | Person appointed by the sponsor to oversee the trial at sites |
| Ethics committee (EC) / institutional review board (IRB) | Independent body protecting the rights, safety and well-being of subjects |
| Subject / participant | Person taking part, either a patient or a healthy volunteer |

## 4.2 Developing a clinical trial protocol

The **protocol** is the document that describes the objectives, design, methods, statistical considerations and organisation of a trial. Every person involved works from it, and the regulator and ethics committee approve it before the trial starts. Changes are made only by formal **protocol amendments**, which also need approval.

### a. Steps in developing a protocol

```text
Define the research question (from pre-clinical data and earlier phases)
 → Literature review and regulatory/scientific advice
 → Choose design, population, endpoints, sample size
 → Draft with clinicians, statisticians, pharmacologists, regulatory, QA
 → Internal review → regulator + ethics committee review → final version
 → Amendments as needed during the trial
```

### b. Contents of a protocol (ICH E6 outline)

1. **General information:** title, protocol number, version and date; names of sponsor, monitor, investigators, laboratories.
2. **Background:** name and description of the investigational product, summary of non-clinical and clinical findings, known risks and benefits, route and dosage, population, references.
3. **Objectives and purpose:** primary and secondary.
4. **Trial design:**
   - primary and secondary **endpoints**;
   - type of trial: placebo-controlled or active-controlled, parallel or crossover;
   - **randomisation** (to avoid selection bias) and **blinding** (open, single-blind, double-blind);
   - treatments and duration; stopping rules; drug accountability; how randomisation codes are kept and broken.
5. **Selection and withdrawal of subjects:** inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, withdrawal criteria and follow-up.
6. **Treatment of subjects:** products, schedule, permitted and prohibited concomitant medicines, compliance checks.
7. **Assessment of efficacy:** parameters, how and when measured.
8. **Assessment of safety:** parameters, recording and reporting of adverse events, follow-up.
9. **Statistics:** sample size with power, significance level, analysis sets (for example intention-to-treat), interim analyses, handling of missing data.
10. **Direct access to source data and documents** for monitoring, audit and inspection.
11. **Quality control and quality assurance.**
12. **Ethics:** ethics committee approval, informed consent.
13. **Data handling and record keeping.**
14. **Financing, insurance, compensation and publication policy.**

### c. Features of a good protocol

Clear and answerable question; scientifically sound design; subjects protected; feasible at the planned sites; consistent with the Investigator's Brochure; enough detail for every site to do the same thing.

## 4.3 Institutional Review Board / Independent Ethics Committee

An **ethics committee** (called an IRB in the USA, IEC or EC elsewhere) is an independent body of medical, scientific and non-scientific members. It reviews and approves the protocol, the informed consent documents and the investigators and facilities, and it keeps watch on the trial to protect the subjects.

### a. Formation (constitution)

**India (NDCT Rules 2019, rule 7)** — an ethics committee for clinical trials must have:

- a **minimum of seven members** from medical, non-medical, scientific and non-scientific areas, with at least:
  - one lay person;
  - one woman member;
  - one legal expert;
  - one independent member from a related field (such as a social scientist, a representative of a voluntary organisation, a philosopher, ethicist or theologian);
- **at least 50% of members not affiliated** with the institute;
- a **chairperson** who is not affiliated with the institute, and a **member secretary** who is affiliated;
- members trained as specified by the Central Licensing Authority.

The committee must be **registered** with the Central Licensing Authority (application in Form CT-01; registration granted in Form CT-02) before it can approve trials. An ethics committee that only approves biomedical and health research (not drug trials) registers with the authority named in the rules for that purpose.

**USA (21 CFR 56):** an IRB has at least five members of varied background, including at least one scientist, one non-scientist and one member not affiliated with the institution; members with a conflict of interest do not vote on that study.

### b. Working procedures

1. Written **standard operating procedures** covering membership, meetings, quorum, review, decisions and records.
2. **Initial review** of the protocol, Investigator's Brochure, informed consent form and patient information in the local language, advertisements for recruitment, investigator CVs, insurance and compensation arrangements.
3. **Decision** in a properly constituted meeting: approval, approval with modifications, disapproval, or termination/suspension of an earlier approval. Members with a conflict of interest withdraw.
4. **Expedited review** for minor amendments, where its SOPs allow.
5. **Continuing review** at intervals suited to the risk (at least yearly in most systems): progress reports, amendments, protocol deviations.
6. **Safety review:** serious adverse events, deaths, new safety information; opinion on compensation for injury or death (India).
7. **Site visits** where needed.
8. **Record keeping:** membership lists, SOPs, minutes, correspondence, kept for the period set by the rules.

## 4.4 Informed consent process and procedures

**Informed consent** is the process by which a subject voluntarily confirms willingness to take part in a trial after being told all aspects of the trial relevant to that decision. It is documented by a written, signed and dated consent form. It is a **process**, not only a signature: it continues throughout the trial.

### a. Essential elements of the information given

1. That the study involves research; its purpose and expected duration.
2. Procedures, including which are experimental; trial treatments and chance of random assignment.
3. Foreseeable risks and discomforts; expected benefits (or that there may be none).
4. Alternative treatments available.
5. Confidentiality of records, and who may see them (monitors, auditors, ethics committee, regulators).
6. Compensation and treatment available for trial-related injury.
7. Whom to contact with questions or in case of injury.
8. That participation is **voluntary**, and the subject may **withdraw at any time** without penalty or loss of benefits.
9. Expected payments or expenses, and the approximate number of subjects.
10. Circumstances in which participation may be ended by the investigator.

### b. Procedure

```text
Approved consent form and information sheet (in a language the subject understands)
 → Investigator or delegate explains the trial in plain words
 → Enough time to read, think, ask questions, consult family
 → No pressure or undue influence
 → Subject (or legally acceptable representative) signs and dates;
   person explaining signs; impartial witness if subject cannot read
 → Copy given to the subject
 → Re-consent when important new information arises
```

### c. Special situations

- **Children:** consent of a parent or legally acceptable representative, plus the child's **assent** when the child can understand.
- **Unconscious or mentally incapable subjects:** consent of a legally acceptable representative; emergency situations as allowed by the rules and ethics committee.
- **Illiterate subjects:** an impartial witness is present throughout.
- **India:** the NDCT Rules require an **audio-video recording** of the informed consent process for vulnerable subjects in clinical trials of a new chemical entity or new molecular entity; for trials of anti-HIV and anti-leprosy drugs, only an audio recording is kept. The checklist of consent elements and a model consent form are in the Third Schedule of the rules.

## 4.5 GCP obligations of investigators, sponsors and monitors

### a. Investigator

1. Is qualified by education, training and experience; has enough time, staff and facilities; has adequate number of eligible subjects available.
2. Follows the approved protocol; documents and explains any deviation.
3. Obtains ethics committee approval before starting and keeps the committee informed.
4. Obtains and documents informed consent before any trial procedure.
5. Provides medical care for adverse events during and after participation.
6. **Reports safety events:** serious adverse events promptly to the sponsor (and, in India, to the regulator and ethics committee — see 4.7).
7. Keeps the investigational product properly: storage, dispensing only to subjects, accountability records, return or destruction.
8. Keeps accurate, complete source documents and case report forms; permits monitoring, audit and inspection.
9. Follows randomisation procedures and breaks the blind only as the protocol allows.
10. Submits progress reports and the final report; keeps essential documents for the required period.

### b. Sponsor

1. Designs the trial and implements **quality management** (risk-based approach).
2. Selects qualified investigators and sites; obtains regulatory permission.
3. Provides the Investigator's Brochure and updates it.
4. Supplies investigational product made under GMP, properly labelled and coded.
5. Arranges **monitoring** and, independently, **audits**.
6. Handles data management, statistics, clinical study reports.
7. **Safety:** evaluates all safety information and reports serious unexpected suspected adverse reactions to regulators, investigators and ethics committees within the set timelines.
8. Provides insurance and **compensation** for trial-related injury or death (in India under the formula of the rules).
9. Registers the trial in a public registry (in India the **Clinical Trials Registry – India, CTRI**, before enrolling the first subject).
10. May transfer duties to a CRO, but remains finally responsible for the quality and integrity of the data.

### c. Monitor (clinical research associate)

Purpose of monitoring: to check that the rights and well-being of subjects are protected, that the trial data are accurate, complete and verifiable from source documents, and that the trial follows the protocol, GCP and the law.

Duties:

1. Acts as the main line of communication between sponsor and investigator.
2. Checks that the investigator and site remain suitable.
3. Checks that informed consent was obtained before participation.
4. **Source data verification:** compares case report forms with hospital and clinic records.
5. Checks investigational product storage, dispensing and accountability.
6. Checks that adverse events are reported in time.
7. Checks that essential documents are kept in the site file.
8. Writes a **monitoring report** after each visit or contact and follows up findings.

## 4.6 Managing and monitoring clinical trials

### a. Stages of trial management

```text
PLANNING        Protocol, CRF design, budget, feasibility, site selection,
                regulator + ethics approvals, CTRI registration, insurance
START-UP        Investigator meeting, site initiation visit, drug supplies,
                randomisation system, training
CONDUCT         Recruitment and consent, treatment and visits, data entry
                (CRF/eCRF), monitoring visits, safety reporting, amendments,
                drug accountability, query resolution
CLOSE-OUT       Last subject last visit, close-out visits, database lock,
                unblinding, statistical analysis
REPORTING       Clinical study report (ICH E3), results to regulator and
                ethics committee, publication, archiving of essential documents
```

### b. Types of monitoring

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| On-site monitoring | Monitor visits the site and checks source documents |
| Centralised (remote) monitoring | Data reviewed centrally to detect unusual patterns, outliers or missing data |
| Risk-based monitoring | Intensity of monitoring set by the risks to subjects and data in each trial or site |

### c. Quality assurance

- **Audit:** systematic, independent check by the sponsor's QA (separate from monitoring) of trial conduct and documents.
- **Inspection:** done by a regulator, at the site, sponsor or CRO.
- **Essential documents:** documents that allow the conduct of a trial and the quality of its data to be evaluated (protocol, consent forms, approvals, CVs, drug records, monitoring reports, SAE reports).
- Common findings: consent problems, protocol deviations, poor drug accountability, unreported adverse events, data not matching source.

### d. Data and safety monitoring board (DSMB)

An independent group of experts, set up by the sponsor for large or high-risk trials, that reviews accumulating safety (and sometimes efficacy) data at intervals and recommends continuing, modifying or stopping the trial.

## 4.7 Pharmacovigilance: safety monitoring in clinical trials

**Pharmacovigilance** is the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or any other drug-related problem (WHO definition). In a trial it means collecting, assessing and reporting every safety finding so subjects are protected and the safety profile is understood before approval.

### a. Definitions (ICH E2A)

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Adverse event (AE) | Any untoward medical occurrence in a subject given a drug; need not be caused by it |
| Adverse drug reaction (ADR) | A noxious and unintended response to a drug where a causal relationship is at least a reasonable possibility |
| Serious AE / ADR | Results in death, is life-threatening, needs or prolongs hospitalisation, causes persistent or significant disability, or is a congenital anomaly / birth defect; also other medically important events |
| Unexpected ADR | Nature or severity not consistent with the reference safety information (Investigator's Brochure or approved label) |
| SUSAR | Suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction |

Severity (mild, moderate, severe) is different from seriousness (the regulatory criteria above).

### b. Safety monitoring process

```text
Subject reports / investigator detects event
 → Record in source and CRF (onset, severity, seriousness, action, outcome)
 → Investigator assesses causality (e.g. WHO-UMC categories) and seriousness
 → Serious → expedited report (see timelines)
 → Sponsor assesses expectedness and causality → SUSAR reported
   to regulator, ethics committees and all investigators
 → Aggregate review: DSMB, safety update reports, IB update
 → Actions: protocol change, consent update, dose change, trial stop
```

### c. Reporting timelines

| System | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| ICH E2A (adopted by many regulators) | Fatal or life-threatening unexpected ADRs: as soon as possible and within **7 calendar days** of first knowledge (follow-up within a further 8 days); other serious unexpected ADRs: within **15 calendar days** |
| India, NDCT Rules 2019 | Investigator reports every **serious adverse event** to the Central Licensing Authority, the sponsor (or its representative) and the ethics committee **within 24 hours** of occurrence; the report after due analysis goes to the Central Licensing Authority, the ethics committee chairperson and the head of the institution **within 14 days**; reasons must be given for any delay. For a death, the authority sets up an independent expert committee to examine the cause and compensation |
| USA, 21 CFR 312.32 | IND safety reports within 15 calendar days; unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected reactions within 7 calendar days |

### d. Other safety tools

- **Development Safety Update Report (DSUR, ICH E2F):** yearly summary of safety during development.
- Updated Investigator's Brochure.
- After approval: periodic safety update reports (in India every six months for the first two years and yearly for the next two years), spontaneous reporting through the **Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)**, whose national coordination centre is the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.

### e. Compensation (India)

The NDCT Rules require the sponsor to give free medical management for injury during a trial, and financial compensation for trial-related injury or death, calculated by the formula in the Seventh Schedule after review by the ethics committee and the Central Licensing Authority. Check the current rule text for amounts and procedure.

## Remember

- Protocol = objectives, design (randomised, blinded, controlled), subjects (inclusion/exclusion), treatment, efficacy, safety, statistics, ethics, data, finance.
- Ethics committee (India): ≥7 members incl. lay person, woman, legal expert, independent member; ≥50% non-affiliated; non-affiliated chairperson; registration CT-01 → CT-02. US IRB ≥5 members.
- Informed consent: voluntary, informed, documented, ongoing; children assent; impartial witness; audio-video recording for vulnerable subjects in NCE/NME trials (audio only for anti-HIV and anti-leprosy).
- Investigator: protocol, consent, care, SAE reporting, drug accountability, records. Sponsor: quality system, sites, IB, GMP supplies, monitoring, safety, compensation, registration (CTRI). Monitor: source data verification, reports.
- Trial stages: planning → start-up → conduct → close-out → reporting (ICH E3); audit vs inspection; DSMB.
- Serious = death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly. ICH: 7 / 15 days. India: SAE 24 hours, analysed report 14 days.

# Unit 5: Regulatory concepts

Regulatory affairs has its own vocabulary and its own reference books. This unit explains the basic terms, the difference between laws, regulations, guidelines and guidance, and four US publications that every regulatory professional uses: the **Federal Register**, the **Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)**, the **Orange Book** and the **Purple Book**. (The syllabus writes "Code of Federal Regulatory"; the correct name is Code of Federal Regulations.) Indian equivalents are given alongside so the ideas can be applied at home.

## 5.1 Basic regulatory terminology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Drug | A substance used for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease, or to affect the structure or function of the body (each law has its own exact definition, e.g. section 3(b) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940) |
| New drug | In India: a drug not yet approved for the proposed use, or an approved drug with new claims, new dosage form, new route, new combination, etc. (NDCT Rules 2019) |
| Investigational product | Active ingredient or placebo being tested or used as a reference in a trial |
| Active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) | The substance that gives the pharmacological effect |
| New chemical entity / new molecular entity (NCE/NME) | An active moiety never approved before |
| Innovator / reference product | The first approved product, used as the comparator for generics |
| Reference listed drug (RLD) | US term for the approved product a generic copies |
| Generic drug | Same API, dosage form, strength, route and use as the reference, and bioequivalent to it |
| Biological product / biologic | Product made from living systems (vaccines, blood products, proteins, antibodies) |
| Biosimilar | Biologic highly similar to an approved reference biologic with no clinically meaningful differences |
| Interchangeable product | US term: a biosimilar that may be substituted for the reference product without the prescriber's intervention, where state law allows |
| Bioavailability / bioequivalence | Rate and extent of absorption / no significant difference in these between two products |
| Sponsor / applicant | Person or company that runs the trial / submits the application |
| Marketing authorisation holder (MAH) | Company legally responsible for the product on the market |
| Dossier | The complete set of documents submitted for approval |
| Label / labelling | Label = matter on the container; labelling = label plus package insert and all printed matter that goes with the product |
| SmPC / PIL | Summary of product characteristics (for professionals) / patient information leaflet (EU terms) |
| Variation / supplement | Application to change an approved product (EU term / US term) |
| Renewal | Re-approval at the end of a validity period (e.g. EU after five years) |
| Clinical hold | FDA order to delay or stop a clinical investigation |
| Complete response letter | FDA letter listing why an application cannot be approved in its present form |
| Tentative approval | US: an ANDA meets all scientific needs but cannot be approved yet because of patents or exclusivity |
| Orphan drug | Drug for a rare disease, with special incentives |
| Exclusivity | Period during which a regulator will not approve (or accept) competing applications, granted by law on approval |
| Patent | Intellectual property right granted by the patent office for an invention, independent of drug approval |
| GxP | Collective name for good practices: GLP (laboratory), GCP (clinical), GMP (manufacturing), GDP (distribution), GVP (pharmacovigilance) |
| Pharmacovigilance | Detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects |
| PSUR / PBRER | Periodic safety update report / periodic benefit-risk evaluation report |
| Regulatory intelligence | Collecting and analysing current regulatory information to guide strategy |

## 5.2 Laws, Acts, regulations, guidelines and guidance

These words describe **levels** of regulatory documents. The higher the level, the stronger its legal force.

```text
        ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ CONSTITUTION                       │
        ├────────────────────────────────────┤
        │ ACT / LAW (statute)                │  passed by Parliament / Congress
        │ e.g. Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940; │  legally binding
        │ US FD&C Act                        │
        ├────────────────────────────────────┤
        │ REGULATIONS / RULES                │  made by the government or agency
        │ e.g. Drugs Rules 1945, NDCT Rules  │  under powers given by the Act;
        │ 2019; US 21 CFR                    │  legally binding
        ├────────────────────────────────────┤
        │ GUIDELINES / GUIDANCE              │  recommendations explaining how
        │ e.g. ICH guidelines, FDA guidance, │  to meet the law; not legally
        │ CDSCO guidance documents           │  binding by themselves
        └────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### a. Law and Act

- A **law** is a rule of conduct made and enforced by the state. An **Act** (statute) is a law passed by the legislature (Parliament in India, Congress in the USA) and signed into force.
- Acts set broad principles, define offences and penalties, create authorities and give the government power to make rules.
- Examples: India — Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, Pharmacy Act 1948, NDPS Act 1985, Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954. USA — Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 1938 and amendments (Kefauver–Harris 1962, Hatch–Waxman 1984), Public Health Service Act.

### b. Regulations (rules)

- **Regulations** are detailed, legally binding requirements made by an executive authority under the power given by an Act ("delegated" or "subordinate" legislation).
- They say exactly what must be done: forms, licences, standards, timelines.
- Examples: India — Drugs Rules 1945, NDCT Rules 2019, Medical Devices Rules 2017. USA — regulations in Title 21 CFR (e.g. 21 CFR 312 for IND, 211 for GMP).
- In the USA new regulations are made by **notice-and-comment rulemaking:** the proposed rule is published in the Federal Register, the public comments, and the final rule is published with a date of effect. In India, draft rules are published in the **Gazette of India** for objections and suggestions, and final rules are notified in the Gazette (as GSR notifications).

### c. Guidelines and guidance

- **Guidelines** are recommendations that describe an acceptable way to meet the legal requirements. They are not law; another approach may be used if it satisfies the law and is justified.
- **FDA guidance documents** represent the FDA's "current thinking" on a topic. They are not binding on the FDA or the public; they use words like "should" and "recommend", while regulations use "must" and "shall". Draft guidances are published for comment before being finalised.
- **ICH guidelines** are harmonised technical guidelines adopted by member regulators: Q (quality, e.g. Q1 stability, Q8–Q10), S (safety, e.g. S7 safety pharmacology), E (efficacy, e.g. E6 GCP, E2A safety reporting), M (multidisciplinary, e.g. M4 CTD). Once a regulator adopts an ICH guideline it becomes part of its expectations.
- **WHO guidelines** (e.g. WHO GMP) are used widely, especially by countries without their own detailed guidance.
- **CDSCO** issues guidance documents and notices (for example on clinical trials, BA/BE studies, biosimilars).

### d. Comparison

| Point | Act / law | Regulation / rule | Guideline / guidance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Made by | Legislature | Government / agency under the Act | Agency or international body |
| Binding | Yes | Yes | No (recommendation) |
| Detail | Broad | Detailed | Technical, practical |
| Change | Slow (amendment by legislature) | By notification after consultation | Easily revised |
| Language | Shall / must | Shall / must | Should / recommended |
| Example | D&C Act 1940; FD&C Act | Drugs Rules 1945; 21 CFR 314 | ICH Q1A; FDA BE guidance |

## 5.3 Federal Register

The **Federal Register (FR)** is the **official daily journal of the US government**. It is published every federal working day by the **Office of the Federal Register** (part of the National Archives and Records Administration) with the US Government Publishing Office.

**Contents (sections):**

1. **Rules and regulations:** final rules, with the date they take effect.
2. **Proposed rules:** draft regulations, with the period for public comments.
3. **Notices:** announcements of guidance documents, advisory committee meetings, availability of documents, decisions on applications, withdrawal of approvals.
4. **Presidential documents:** executive orders and proclamations.

**Importance in drug regulation:**

- It is how the public learns of proposed and final FDA regulations, and how comments are invited.
- It gives the legal history ("preamble") explaining the reasons behind each regulation.
- Citations are by volume and page, written like "65 FR 1776".
- Final rules published in the FR are later collected ("codified") into the CFR.

**Indian equivalent:** the **Gazette of India**, in which drug rules, amendments, bans and other notifications are published (for example the NDCT Rules 2019 were notified as G.S.R. 227(E)).

## 5.4 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)

The **CFR** is the **codification (organised collection) of the general and permanent rules** published in the Federal Register by US federal agencies. It is divided into **50 titles**, each covering a broad area; drug rules are in **Title 21 — Food and Drugs**. Each title is revised once a year (Title 21 as of 1 April), and an electronic version (eCFR) is kept up to date continuously.

**Structure and citation:**

```text
Title → Chapter → Subchapter → Part → Subpart → Section
21 CFR 312.40  =  Title 21, Part 312, Section 40
(Chapter I of Title 21 = Food and Drug Administration, Parts 1–1299)
```

**Important parts of 21 CFR for pharmacy students:**

| Part | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 11 | Electronic records and electronic signatures |
| 50 | Protection of human subjects (informed consent) |
| 54 | Financial disclosure by clinical investigators |
| 56 | Institutional review boards |
| 58 | Good laboratory practice for non-clinical studies |
| 201 | Labelling |
| 210, 211 | Current good manufacturing practice (general; finished pharmaceuticals) |
| 312 | Investigational new drug application |
| 314 | Applications for FDA approval to market a new drug (NDA, ANDA) |
| 320 | Bioavailability and bioequivalence requirements |
| 600–680 | Biological products |
| 820 | Quality system / quality management for medical devices |

**FR vs CFR:**

| Federal Register | Code of Federal Regulations |
| --- | --- |
| Daily journal, in date order | Organised by subject (title and part) |
| Contains proposed rules, final rules, notices | Contains only final, permanent rules in force |
| Includes preambles explaining rules | Rule text only |
| Like a newspaper of the government | Like an encyclopaedia of the rules |

## 5.5 Orange Book

**Official title:** *Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations*, published by the FDA (named after its orange cover). It is available online, and its data files are updated monthly.

### a. What it contains

1. A list of drug products approved by the FDA as safe and effective under the FD&C Act (NDA and ANDA products).
2. **Therapeutic equivalence (TE) evaluations** for multi-source prescription products.
3. **Patent information** listed by NDA holders for each product.
4. **Exclusivity information** for each product.
5. Lists of OTC products and of discontinued products.

### b. Therapeutic equivalence codes

| First letter | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Considered therapeutically equivalent to other pharmaceutically equivalent products | **AB** — bioequivalence actual or potential problems resolved by adequate in vivo/in vitro evidence; AA — products in conventional dosage forms with no known BE problems; AN, AO, AP, AT for aerosols, oils, parenterals, topicals |
| **B** | Not considered therapeutically equivalent at present (BE not shown or problems not resolved) | BC, BD, BE, BN, BP, BR, BS, BT, BX |

### c. Uses

- Pharmacists and states use TE codes to decide **generic substitution** (an AB-rated generic may be substituted).
- Generic companies use it to choose the **RLD** and reference standard, and to find **patents and exclusivities** they must certify against (Paragraph I–IV).
- It is the starting point for planning a generic launch.

### d. Common US exclusivities shown in it (well-established figures)

| Exclusivity | Period |
| --- | --- |
| New chemical entity | 5 years |
| New clinical investigation (e.g. new indication supported by new studies) | 3 years |
| Orphan drug | 7 years |
| Paediatric | Adds 6 months to existing patents/exclusivities |
| First generic with Paragraph IV challenge | 180 days |

## 5.6 Purple Book

**What it is:** the FDA's *Database of Licensed Biological Products*, the biologics counterpart of the Orange Book. It lists biological products licensed under the **Public Health Service Act** by CDER and CBER.

**Contents:**

1. Licensed biological products (BLAs under section 351(a)) and their reference products.
2. **Biosimilar** products (section 351(k)) and whether each is also **interchangeable**.
3. Date of licensure.
4. **Reference product exclusivity** expiry dates and any interchangeability exclusivity.
5. Certain patent information (added by later law).

**Uses:** helps prescribers, pharmacists and companies know which biosimilars exist, which are interchangeable (and so may be substituted where state law allows), and when exclusivity ends.

### Orange Book vs Purple Book

| Point | Orange Book | Purple Book |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Products | Small-molecule drugs (NDA, ANDA) | Biological products (BLA, biosimilars) |
| Law | FD&C Act | Public Health Service Act |
| Equivalence term | Therapeutic equivalence (A/B codes) | Biosimilarity and interchangeability |
| Copies | Generics | Biosimilars |
| Patent and exclusivity data | Yes | Exclusivity dates and certain patent information |

## 5.7 Linking the concepts

```text
Act (FD&C Act / D&C Act 1940)
   └─→ Regulations (21 CFR / Drugs Rules, NDCT Rules) — first published in
       the Federal Register / Gazette of India, then codified (CFR)
          └─→ Guidance (FDA guidance, ICH, CDSCO guidance) — how to comply
                 └─→ Applications (IND, NDA, ANDA, BLA / CT-04, CT-18, CT-21)
                        └─→ Approved products listed in the Orange Book or
                            Purple Book; generics/biosimilars refer to them
```

## Remember

- Act (legislature, binding, broad) → regulations/rules (agency, binding, detailed) → guidelines/guidance (recommendations, "should", not binding).
- Federal Register: daily journal of the US government; rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents; India's equivalent is the Gazette of India.
- CFR: 50 titles; Title 21 Food and Drugs; parts 11, 50, 56, 58, 210/211, 312, 314, 320; revised yearly (Title 21 as of 1 April); citation 21 CFR 312.40.
- Orange Book: "Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations"; TE codes A (AB etc.) and B; patents and exclusivity; data files updated monthly.
- Exclusivity: NCE 5 years, new clinical investigation 3 years, orphan 7 years, paediatric +6 months, first Paragraph IV generic 180 days.
- Purple Book: Database of Licensed Biological Products; PHS Act 351(a) and 351(k); biosimilar and interchangeable; reference product exclusivity.
